claims.text: A nanohierarchical microstructure with nanoprecipitates in CoCrFeNi can maintain low friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
Severe plastic deformation followed by controlled annealing, or modified mechanical alloying, will introduce nanoscale composition undulations and nanoprecipitates into CoCrFeNi.
The resulting nanoprecipitates may be nanoscale ordered phases or fine oxides.
The proposed tests span approximately 25 °C to 800 °C in ambient air under a load of about 1 N.
The intervention will produce nano-coupled grains with evenly dispersed, coherent nanoprecipitates.
The nanohierarchical architecture can dynamically adapt the friction interface.
At low temperature, multiple deformation pathways in the nanostructured interface release frictional stress.
At high temperature, the nanoprecipitates coalesce into a dense self-forming glaze layer.
The high-temperature glaze layer minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
The adaptive interface mitigates temperature-induced changes in both friction and wear.
Modified CoCrFeNi may have a coefficient of friction about 30% below that of conventionally processed CoCrFeNi across the full temperature range.
Modified CoCrFeNi may have a wear rate up to one order of magnitude below that of conventionally processed CoCrFeNi across the full temperature range.
Conventionally processed CoCrFeNi typically has higher and more temperature-variable friction coefficients and wear rates between room temperature and 800 °C.
Oxidation is active under the specified ambient-air sliding conditions.
Prior evidence shows that a nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation can provide ultralow wear from room temperature to 800 °C in another complex concentrated alloy.
The exact improvement and optimal CoCrFeNi processing parameters remain undetermined.
A controlled comparison will use conventional and nanohierarchically processed samples from the same CoCrFeNi batch under identical sliding conditions.

The hypothesis will be refuted if the intervention fails to produce statistically significant reductions in both friction and wear across the tested temperatures and fails to form the expected adaptive layer.
